issues.legal_issue: A notice that demands payment of arrears and purports to terminate a month-to-month tenancy is ineffective to terminate the tenancy if it gives fewer than fifteen clear days’ notice.
material_facts: The tenancy was from month to month.
The landlords’ notice demanded payment of arrears within one month and stated that they would file an ejectment suit if payment was not made; it also required the tenant to vacate.
The tenant received the notice with only fourteen clear days before the stated termination date.
issues.conclusion: The notice could be construed as a composite notice for the statutory rent-demand requirement and for termination of the tenancy, but it was ineffective to terminate the tenancy because it did not give fifteen clear days’ notice.
issues.legal_principle: Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 requires fifteen days’ notice to terminate a month-to-month tenancy. The notice period is calculated by excluding the day of service. The Court approved Subadini v. Durga Charan Lal and Gobinda Chandra Saha v. Dwarka Nath Patita, and distinguished Harihar Banerji v. Ramsashi Roy, which concerned the description of the premises rather than the minimum notice period.

predicates.landlord_brought_tenant_eviction_proceed: A landlord brought a proceeding to evict a tenant.
predicates.tenancy_was_month_to_month: The tenant held the premises under a month-to-month tenancy.
predicates.notice_combined_rent_demand_with_termina: The landlord’s notice both demanded payment of arrears and communicated an intention to terminate the tenancy if payment was not made.
predicates.notice_gave_fewer_than_fifteen_clear_day: The tenant received fewer than fifteen clear days’ notice before the stated termination date.

issues.definition: If a landlord brings an eviction proceeding against a month-to-month tenant after using a combined rent-demand and termination notice that gives fewer than fifteen clear days, the notice does not terminate the tenancy.

issues.legal_issue: A later notice requiring a tenant to vacate is effective to terminate a month-to-month tenancy when it gives more than fifteen clear days’ notice and the eviction suit is based on that notice.
material_facts: After accepting and cashing the tenant’s cheque, the landlords gave a fresh notice requiring the tenant to vacate by the end of the month.
The fresh notice gave more than fifteen clear days to vacate.
The eviction suit was based on the fresh notice, and the tenant did not vacate.
issues.conclusion: The fresh notice was valid under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and the suit based on it was competently instituted.
issues.legal_principle: Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 requires fifteen days’ notice to terminate a month-to-month tenancy. A notice giving more than fifteen clear days satisfies that requirement.

rule.if: landlord_brought_tenant_eviction_proceeding and tenancy_was_month_to_month and suit_was_based_on_vacate_notice and notice_gave_more_than_fifteen_clear_days

predicates.landlord_brought_tenant_eviction_proceed: A landlord brought a proceeding to evict a tenant.
predicates.tenancy_was_month_to_month: The tenant held the premises under a month-to-month tenancy.
predicates.suit_was_based_on_vacate_notice: The landlord based the eviction proceeding on a notice requiring the tenant to vacate.
predicates.notice_gave_more_than_fifteen_clear_days: The notice gave the tenant more than fifteen clear days to vacate.

issues.definition: When a landlord brings an eviction proceeding against a month-to-month tenant based on a vacate notice that gives more than fifteen clear days, the notice validly terminates the tenancy.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord relying on a tenant’s failure to pay arrears within the notice period need not prove that rent remained in arrears on the date the eviction suit was filed.
material_facts: The tenant was in arrears of rent.
The landlords gave written notice demanding payment within one month.
The tenant failed to pay the arrears within one month after service of the notice.
The tenant later paid the arrears and rent due through a later date, and the landlords accepted the payment before filing suit.
issues.conclusion: The arrears ground was established by the tenant’s failure to pay within one month of service of the demand notice; the ground did not have to subsist on the date of suit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(a) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1955 requires proof that the tenant was in arrears, received one month’s notice to pay, and failed to pay within that month. Its language does not require arrears to remain outstanding when suit is filed. The Court rejected an interpretation that would add such a condition, distinguished the more extensive tenant protections under other rent laws, and noted that the 1961 Madhya Pradesh Act adopted a different scheme. Sections 16 and 17 of the 1961 Act did not support the proposed interpretation.

rule.if: landlord_brought_statutory_eviction_suit and arrears_existed_when_demanded and landlord_gave_written_payment_demand and tenant_failed_to_pay_within_notice_period

predicates.landlord_brought_statutory_eviction_suit: A landlord brought an eviction proceeding relying on a statutory ground based on non-payment of rent.
predicates.arrears_existed_when_demanded: The tenant owed rent when the landlord demanded payment.
predicates.landlord_gave_written_payment_demand: The landlord gave the tenant a written demand allowing one month to pay the arrears.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_pay_within_notice_perio: The tenant did not pay the arrears within the period allowed by the demand notice.

issues.definition: If a landlord brings a statutory eviction proceeding after the tenant owed rent, received a written demand allowing one month to pay, and failed to pay in time, the arrears need not still be outstanding when suit is filed.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s acceptance of rent after a tenant’s failure to pay arrears within the demand period does not, by itself, waive the statutory eviction ground when the tenancy has continued.
material_facts: The tenant failed to pay the arrears within one month after receiving the demand notice.
The first notice was ineffective to terminate the tenancy.
The landlords cashed a cheque that included both the arrears and rent due for later months while the landlord-tenant relationship continued.
The landlords later gave a separate vacate notice and based the suit on that notice.
issues.conclusion: Acceptance of the cheque did not, by itself, waive the landlords’ right to rely on the statutory ground arising from the tenant’s default; nor did it waive the right arising from the later vacate notice.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied section 4(a) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1955 and section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Because the first notice did not validly terminate the tenancy, the tenant remained liable for rent and the landlords could accept it without that act alone waiving the separate statutory right arising from the default. The Court held that illustration (a) to section 113 of the Transfer of Property Act did not apply. It also held that acceptance of rent before the later vacate notice did not, by itself, waive the right arising from that later notice.

predicates.landlord_brought_tenant_eviction_proceed: A landlord brought a proceeding to evict a tenant.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_pay_arrears_within_noti: The tenant did not pay arrears within the period allowed by the landlord’s demand notice.
predicates.tenancy_continued_when_rent_was_accepted: The landlord-tenant relationship had not ended when the landlord accepted rent.
predicates.landlord_accepted_rent_after_default: The landlord accepted rent after the tenant had failed to pay the demanded arrears in time.

issues.definition: When a landlord accepts rent after a tenant’s untimely payment while the tenancy continues, that acceptance alone does not waive the statutory eviction ground arising from the default.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory ground that permits eviction does not itself terminate a periodic tenancy or convert non-payment into a forfeiture of the lease.
material_facts: The tenant occupied the premises under a month-to-month tenancy.
The landlord relied on the tenant’s failure to pay arrears within the period allowed by a demand notice.
The parties’ landlord-tenant relationship continued until a valid termination notice was given.
issues.conclusion: The statutory arrears ground only removed the statutory bar to exercising the landlord’s ordinary right to terminate the tenancy; it did not change the periodic character of the tenancy or create a right of re-entry for forfeiture. Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 therefore did not apply as a relief against forfeiture.
issues.legal_principle: The Court read section 4(a) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1955 together with section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The statutory ground conditions the landlord’s ordinary right to terminate; it does not turn a periodic tenancy into a fixed or indefinite tenancy or add a re-entry condition. The Court considered forfeiture under section 111(g) and relief under section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and held that the statutory arrears ground did not constitute such a forfeiture.

predicates.landlord_brought_tenant_eviction_proceed: A landlord brought a proceeding to evict a tenant.
predicates.tenancy_was_periodic: The tenant held the premises under a tenancy that renewed periodically.
predicates.statutory_eviction_ground_was_establishe: The landlord established a statutory ground that permits seeking the tenant’s eviction.

issues.definition: If a landlord establishes a statutory eviction ground against a tenant in a periodic tenancy, that ground only removes the bar to ordinary termination and does not itself terminate the tenancy or create a forfeiture.
